lakeHero.audience: For disaster teams in Gilgit-Baltistan and upper Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.
lakeHero.title: Glacial lakes through the clouds, seen by radar
lakeHero.lede: This shows how often NISAR radar observed each glacial lake while clouds blocked optical satellites. It shows whether the radar water area moved beyond its own noise.
lakeHero.screening: Indicative screening on provisional NISAR data. Official warnings come from PMD, NDMA, GBDMA and PDMA.
lakeHero.headlineSource: A valid look is one lake seen on one NISAR pass that passed the checks on How we know. Provisional data.

beats.label: The cloud gap
beats.title: Clouds hid the lakes after 16 June

quote.text: Persistent cloud cover after 16 June 2026 has limited the availability of cloud-free satellite imagery, making it difficult to accurately assess lake area changes during the last three to four days.

body: NISAR is a radar satellite, so cloud does not stop it. Between {cloud_start} and {cloud_end} it made {cloud_looks} valid looks across {cloud_lakes} of the {lake_count} lakes on this list.
A valid look is one lake seen on one NISAR pass that passed our checks. It does not measure change. Lake Watch gives the change for each lake, with the date, the look count and the noise.
noData: NISAR is a radar satellite, so cloud does not stop it. Lake data is not in this build, so no counts are shown here.

beats.label: How radar sees lakes
beats.title: Calm water is dark, and shadow falls on the valley walls
body: Calm water acts like a mirror for radar. The beam bounces away from the satellite, so little comes back and the lake looks dark.

Steep mountains can look dark too. Where a slope faces away from the satellite, the radar cannot see the ground behind the ridge. That radar shadow is dark. A slope facing the satellite folds over (layover) and looks bright.

Shadow and layover fall on the valley walls, almost never on a flat lake. SARtale smooths the speckle. Inside the lake zone, a pixel is water when its HH is at least 3 dB darker than the median of the 6 km window. A terrain model maps walls in shadow or layover. SARtale excludes these walls from that median.
Wet shore and exposed mud read as water too. A lake drawing down onto its own flats barely changes its radar area. How we know gives the thresholds.

beats.label: Lake Watch
beats.title: Lake Watch: one level for each lake
body: Lake Watch lists {watch_list}. A measured lake has a level: No change, Watch, Alert: growing, or Decrease noted. Otherwise its status says why there is none: Frozen (likely), Frozen (seen by Sentinel-2), Break-up likely, Not seen this pass, Not observable, Not measurable, Not yet validated against Sentinel-2, Not enough NISAR looks yet, or No lake now.

Each pass is compared with the median of earlier passes on its own track and that track's noise. One pass beyond {change_factor} times the noise is a Watch. Two in a row growing, on any tracks, are an Alert: growing. Two in a row falling are a Decrease noted, for information only, because radar sees a lake drawing down onto wet sediment at only a tenth to a fifth of its size. Every Watch, Alert and Decrease noted carries a short message: what changed, how sure, what it is not, and what to do.

Frozen (likely) comes from air temperature at the lake, and Frozen (seen by Sentinel-2) from a clear optical image. Radar cannot tell new ice from open water. Frozen ground around a lake can read as water. A frozen lake gets no level until it thaws.

No lake now marks a site where recent imagery shows no lake, such as the empty basin of an ice-dammed lake that has drained. It gets no level, and its dark radar area is not counted as lake area. The site stays on the list to monitor whether a lake forms.
Control lakes, kept to check the method, are listed last.
noData: Lake data is not in this build. Lake Watch lists each lake with a status once data/lakes.json is present.

beats.label: Limits and next steps
beats.title: What this does not tell you, and what comes next
body: This is indicative screening on provisional NISAR data. Official warnings come from PMD, NDMA, GBDMA and PDMA.

A level compares a lake only with its own earlier passes. Areas count water inside each lake's outline or search circle, wet shore included. An Alert is for slow-growth monitoring, not outburst warning. It comes 5–12 days after a change begins. A drawdown onto wet sediment is nearly invisible. Frozen lakes, lakes under 0.05 km² and wind-roughened water are not validated. In the Sentinel-2 cross-check, radar water {optical_overlap}, one date per lake. So it is not a validation of lake extent.

The SARtale team wants to agree these next steps with the administration. They are SUPARCO's lake IDs and locations, so areas can be compared, and which lakes district teams most need on the list. They also include ground reports from those teams and a re-run when NASA reprocesses the files.
